concept.body: Cross-section patterns identify and size solids: constant congruent circles mean a cylinder, circles shrinking to a point (at the similarity ratio of heights) mean a cone, and circles in every direction mean a sphere — whose largest section, the great circle through the center, carries the true radius, with off-center slices shrinking by π(R² − d²).

explanationVariants: Slices shrink steadily to a point — the cone's signature.

widget.prompt: Parallel slices of a solid are circles that shrink steadily to a single point at the top. The solid is:

options.label: A cone
options.feedback: Steady shrink to the apex — similarity at work, the cone's fingerprint.

options.label: A cylinder
options.feedback: Cylinders keep slices CONSTANT — shrinking says cone.

options.label: A sphere
options.feedback: A sphere grows then shrinks, and never linearly — the steady shrink to a point is the cone.

options.label: A cube
options.feedback: A cube's parallel slices are constant squares — shrinking circles say cone.

steps.body: Sections are evidence. A solid's slice pattern identifies it (all circles ⇒ sphere; constant congruent circles ⇒ cylinder; shrinking-to-a-point circles ⇒ cone), sizes it (a great circle exposes the true radius), and — next chapter — will price its volume. Reading slices IS reading solids.

explanationVariants: Parallel slices all congruent ⇒ straight walls; circular ⇒ round base.
Congruent circles at every height: a cylinder.

widget.prompt: Every slice of a solid parallel to its base is a circle congruent to the base. The solid is:

options.label: A cylinder
options.feedback: Constancy is the cylinder's testimony; the cone would shrink, the sphere would bulge and shrink.

options.label: A cone
options.feedback: A cone's parallel slices SHRINK toward the apex — congruent slices say cylinder.

options.label: A sphere
options.feedback: A sphere's slices grow to the equator then shrink — constant slices say cylinder.

options.label: A square prism
options.feedback: Its constant sections are SQUARES — circular ones say cylinder.

explanationVariants: The great circle carries the sphere's true radius: C = 2πr = 12π gives r.

widget.prompt: A sphere's great circle has circumference 12π. The sphere's volume coefficient (of π) = ?

numericErrors.feedback: 144 = 12² squares the circumference's coefficient — first r = 6, then (4/3)(6³) = 288.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

explanationVariants: Slice area π(R² − d²) falls as d grows — largest at d = 0.
The claim is exactly the great-circle maximality.

widget.prompt: Why is the great circle the LARGEST section of a sphere?

options.label: Its area is greatest when d = 0.
options.feedback: The chapter's Pythagorean slice formula settles it in one line — every off-center plane pays a d² penalty.

options.label: Its circumference is longest to walk.
options.feedback: That's circumference intuition — the AREA argument is π(R² − d²) maximized at d = 0.

options.label: Slanted slices can be larger.
options.feedback: Every planar slice of a sphere is a circle obeying the same distance formula — none beats d = 0.

options.label: The sphere's symmetry guarantees it.
options.feedback: Symmetry says slices are circles; the SIZE ranking needs π(R² − d²), maximized at the center.

predict.prompt: A cone is cut by a plane parallel to its base, halfway up. How does that slice's AREA compare with the base?

options.label: One quarter of it — the radius halves, so the area quarters
Half of it — halfway up, half the area
The same — parallel cuts of a cone are congruent

predict.reveal: One quarter. Halfway up, the radius has halved — and area follows the SQUARE of the radius, so it drops to a quarter. This is the k² rule appearing inside a single solid. Sweep the plane and watch the area fall faster than the height.

widget.prompt: Sweep the section plane up the cone and stop halfway. Watch how much faster the area shrinks than the height climbs.
widget.successFeedback: Halfway up, the radius is 4 and the area is π(4²) ≈ 50.27 — exactly a quarter of the base's π(8²). Height scaled by ½; area scaled by ½². The exponent is not a rule here, it is something the readout did.
widget.positionFeedback: Not at the halfway cut yet — keep moving and compare the area readout against the base area as you go.
widget.comparisonFeedback: Add the comparison solid to finish the reading.
widget.invariantFeedback: Test more heights first — the point is the RATE the area falls, and one slice cannot show a rate.

widget.prompt: A cylinder and a square prism have the same height, and the square's side equals the cylinder's diameter. Slicing both parallel to their bases at the same height:

options.label: The circle-to-square area ratio stays π/4.
options.feedback: πr² against (2r)² = 4r² gives π/4 at every level — a constant-ratio fact Cavalieri's principle turns into a volume ratio next chapter.

options.label: The circle becomes larger near the top.
options.feedback: Both sections are constant with height — the ratio stays πr² : 4r² = π/4 forever.

options.label: The two sections remain congruent.
options.feedback: A circle never equals a square — but their areas keep the fixed ratio π/4.

options.label: The section areas cannot be compared.
options.feedback: Slice areas compare fine: πr² vs 4r², ratio π/4 at every height.

hints: Work the slice formula at both heights: the pattern π(R² − d²) is the sphere's fingerprint.
At d = 0 the area is 100π — that names R².
explanationVariants: 100π at the center gives R = 10; at 8 up: π(100 − 64) = 36π — slice radius 6, the 6-8-10 again.

widget.prompt: A sphere-shaped tank's widest horizontal section (through the center) has area 100π. What is the area coefficient (of π) of the section 8 units above the center?

numericErrors.feedback: 100 is the great circle — 8 up, the slice pays the d² penalty: 100 − 64 = 36.
64 is d², the penalty itself — the remaining area coefficient is 100 − 64 = 36.
6 is the slice's RADIUS — its area coefficient is 36.

widget.explorationFeedback: Inspect the required exact-number states before checking.

takeaways: Patterns identify: constant circles ⇒ cylinder, shrinking ⇒ cone (similarity runs the rate), all-circles ⇒ sphere.
A great circle exposes the true radius; off-center slices pay π(R² − d²).
Constant slice RATIOS (circle-in-square = π/4) will become volume ratios next.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: Cavalieri's principle — equal slices at every height, equal volumes.
